title: Embouchure: biting the reed versus double lip
summary: Chalini taught him not to put the lip over the teeth; they compare the French double embouchure and Bigard.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well Manuel Mineta talks a lot about Manuel Mineta studied clarinet with Sam Dutre. We'd been on the boat years ago. Oh yeah. When Louie first started out in 18, 18 or so. Uh huh.
Is that right? Sam Dutre taught him to use the double embouchure. How did you learn? Did you cover your upper teeth too?
Yeah. That's the same way that Mr. Charlin taught me.

That's right. He said never put your lip over your top teeth because you would always have a tendency to cut it. And I had noticed that some of the fellas had used that particular system even later in years. And how they managed to blow like that I do not know.
It was supposed to be a French system. And Manuel Mineta says if you bite onto your teeth you're going to wear your teeth down, which some of them do. That's right.
If you know of some of the musicians who play with an instrument, there's an arch in their
Yeah. And just like some of the fellas that blows a trumpet or trombone you know so they have the corn on that. Yeah. But I had-
Bobby Bigard uses that double embouchure and some of the French players do too.
Uh huh. Well one thing he got good results out of it because he was a pretty powerful man for a long time.
